sections.note: This course introduces students to some basic ideas in philosophy and some typical approaches to doing philosophy. Philosophy is an ancient and sprawling area of study. There are many ways to introduce it to students and many ways for students to learn it. This course is framed around the sub-fields called “philosophy of religion” and “philosophy of science.” In the first half of the course, we will consider questions in philosophy of religion, such as how much evidence does one need in order to believe that God exists and is it possible for God to exist given that there is evil in the world. In the second half of the course, we will consider questions in philosophy of science, such as whether inductive reasoning is justified (and if so, how) and what makes something a law of nature. Along the way, we will develop general tools for doing philosophy.

This course is an introduction to some of philosophy’s central problems. Students will learn how to responsibly interpret philosophical texts and learn about philosophy’s relevance for today’s issues and for living a meaningful life. Course topics include living a meaningful life, skepticism, certainty, and biases in knowledge, whether “good” and “bad” actions (like stealing) are culture-dependent, what role love, sex, and friendships have in living a good life, and how to evaluate and make decisions about real-life ethical scenarios (e.g., mass surveillance and marital affairs).

This course introduces students to central questions in moral philosophy. The course is divided into three parts. In the first part, we discuss two topics in applied ethics: whether we have a moral obligation to help people suffering from famine and whether abortion is morally permissible. These questions raise a further issue about the structure of moral responsibility, namely whether there is an important ethical difference between actively doing something and merely allowing something to happen. We will examine this question with the help of a number of well-known trolley cases and related thought experiments. Our discussions in the first part of the course presuppose that we make particular moral judgments. For example, one argument rests on the claim that we have a perfect moral obligation to help a drowning child when we can do so at little cost. In the second part of the course, we take a step back and ask a more fundamental question: is there a general moral principle that can explain and unify our particular moral judgments? To address this question, we will consider two influential moral theories: utilitarianism and Kantian ethics. In the final part of the course, we turn to the connection between ethics and politics. If moral principles guide our actions as individuals, the question arises whether and how they should also guide the institutions that structure our society. We will focus on a particular part of our social life; the economy. According to which principles should the economic benefit and burdens be generated and distributed? Should economic outcomes be guided only by supply and demand, and profic maximization, or are there ethical considerations that should shape a just and beneficial economy?

Ethics is often divided into three subfields: metaethics, normative ethics, and practical ethics. In this class, we will start with questions in metaethics, thinking about questions like, “Is what’s right and wrong dependent on what culture or society you belong to?” and “Is there a single, true morality?” We will then move on to normative ethics, thinking about questions like “What makes actions like slavery and genocide morally wrong?” Finally, we will move on to practical ethics, where we will think about a number of different issues, applying what we previously learned. Some of the issues we will touch on include the morality of abortion, the moral status of animals, the wrongness of sweatshop labor, and the obligation of Western nations to aid developing nations.

This is a survey course in social and political philosophy. In particular, we first explore different kinds of government, the sources of legitimacy that the governing body has, and whether justice can exist only in a well-governed society. Afterwards, we will turn to the question concerning the relationship the government should have with its citizens: what counts as a good citizen, and what counts as civic virtues? Some specific case studies include when and how citizens hold political authorities accountable, and so, we will additionally theorize about how to engage in civil disobedience and other forms of political resistance, such as protesting, boycotting, and more. We will then consider questions on how the history of oppression and our social and cultural identities complicate the baseline of being a good citizen. Finally, we will not only reflect on gender and race, but also certain political practices and labor that are implicitly imposed on citizens, particularly the case of marriage, as articulated by Professor Elizabeth Brake’s work on the politics of marriage:amatonormativity, polyamory, child-rearing, and property division in divorce.

Survey of the leading living religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; examination of basic texts and of philosophic theological elaborations of each religion. How should one live in the digital age? What is the internet doing to attention, education, relationships, and politics? The course pursues answers through studying classic texts in the philosophy of technology.

PHILOSOPHY IN LITERATURE: THE MEANING OF LIFE We will examine key issues surrounding the meaning of life via close readings of literary works by Camus, Dostoevsky, Kafka, Tolstoy, among many others. The course’s themes encompass subjective versus objective meaning, God, suffering, death, freedom, identity and alienation, happiness and morality, the present, culture, intimate others, and, finally, the course of a life.

What is reasoning? What makes an argument strong? How can formal tools help us understand the nature of arguments? This course seeks to answer questions such as these by using symbolic and mathematical tools. In particular, we will explore formal languages, which will allow us to symbolize natural language sentences in a rigorous and mathematically precise way. We begin with a discussion of propositional logic (also known as truth-functional logic). We cover the standard “truth table” semantics for propositional logic and develop a natural-deduction style proof system. Along the way, we will also discuss non-classical logics such as intuitionistic logic. Following our treatment of propositional logic, we explore first-order logic with identity, which allows us to symbolize sentences with quantifier expressions “for all” and “there exists”.
The course is a study of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Cynics, and the Stoics. The main theme is the Socratic legacy concerning the relationship between philosophical inquiry and the good life.

What is the relationship between the mind and the body? What types of things exist? What are their fundamental natures? The course focuses on the metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and epistemology of some of the influential thinkers from the Early Modern era, including Rene Descartes, Elisabeth of Bohemia, Margaret Cavendish, Nicolas Malebranche, Baruch Spinoza, and Gottfried Leibniz.

Ethics and the Good Life - How should one live? In this course, “Ethics and the Good Life,” we will survey a strand of thinking in the Western cultural and intellectual tradition according to which, first, philosophy can answer this question, and second, that it can do so by providing an ethical theory: a systematic account of the sorts of considerations to which one must be receptive and responsive in order to live well. We will begin with some more recent, distinctively modern examples of ethical philosophy in this vein by reading Mill in Utilitarianism, as well as Kant in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals and the Critique of Practical Reason. We will then turn towards less recent and less familiar examples of ethical philosophy by reading selections from Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologica, as well as Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics and Plato’s Republic. We will see that over time, the conception of an adequate answer to our initial question “how should one live?” has itself changed, and we will try to think about what an adequate ethical philosophy looks like, whether it needs to involve the provision of a theory, and, indeed, whether philosophy can answer this question at all.

Can machines think? What is thinking anyway? What is consciousness? Could we merge with machines, and have we already? Could intelligent machines take over? These are some of the questions we will investigate together in this class. This course is an introduction to the philosophy of mind and philosophy of AI. The course will introduce students to theories of and objections to machine thinking, theories of mind and personal identity, theories of consciousness, and arguments for existential risks from artificial intelligence.

Science is one of the world's most successful enterprises, yet we live in an era of unprecedented public distrust in its findings. This course challenges this tension by exploring the foundations and history of scientific inquiry. Does science aim at absolute truth or merely high probability? And is it possible for science to be free of social and political values? This course is structured around two main modules. First, we explore metaphysical and epistemological issues. Starting with the demarcation problem we will ask what differentiates science from pseudoscience (i.e., eugenics and scientific racism)? This motivates issues concerning evidence, predictive success, hypotheses, and confirmation. In addition to weighing the strengths of various inferential models (hypothetico-deduction, inference to best explanation, enumerative induction, etc.), we will also discuss serious puzzles and paradoxes, such as the problem of confirmation and induction, the Raven Paradox, and Bayesian confirmation theory. We will end the unit by comparing theories on method and scientific progress, such as whether scientific progress is rational, how progress can be measured, and whether the standard of measurement is mind-independent. Some specific cases we will examine include the Newtonian revolution, the rise of Darwinism, and Mendelian inheritance. The second module will concern social and political influences in the sciences. Specifically, we will evaluate arguments for and against the possibility of a ‘value-free’ ideal in science, looking closely at what research incentives, the politics of resource distribution among competing research groups, and the human factors behind scientific disasters, such as Chernobyl and the Challenger explosion. Crucially, we will additionally analyze the implications value-laden science has for diversifying the demographic composition of research groups, medical staff, and academic departments. The course concludes by turning toward the crises in public trust and the emerging role of citizen science. Some authors we will read include Philip Kitcher, Liam Kofi-Bright, Kathleen Okruhlik, Mirian Solomon, and Sean A. Valles

Graduate Section This course explores four—two classical and two contemporary—ethical theories, namely those of Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Hannah Arendt, and Simone de Beauvoir. As we work our way through these theories, we will pay special attention to these thinkers’ conceptions of human nature/the human condition and ethics. We start with Aristotle’s related theories as he presents them in the Nicomachean Ethics before looking at Hannah Arendt’s account of The Human Condition. We then turn to Kant’s accounts of human nature and ethics in Religion within the Boundaries of mere Reason and The Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals before finishing up by exploring these themes with the help of Simone de Beauvoir’s The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex.

Graduate Section What is the relation between the mind and the body? Do we have free will? What makes you "you"? These are some of the questions we will investigate together in this class. This course is a survey of topics in the philosophy of mind and consciousness, theories of personal identity, and theories of free will.

Graduate Section The goal of this class is to give you a better understanding of the methodology of metaphysical inquiry and to help you think better when it comes to matters metaphysical. The topics we will investigate are as follows: being, properties, parts and wholes, time, and critiques of metaphysics.

What are the limits of logical proof? How do we formally define the notion of truth? What can(not) be described using formal languages? This course provides an introduction to metalogic, understood as the study of formal systems. A formal system consists of a formal language, a collection of inference rules, and often a semantics which is said to provide that language with meaning. Instead of proving things within a given formal system, metalogic aims to prove things \emph{about} formal systems. One of the goals of metalogic is to explore what we can conclude about particular formal systems--their scope, limits, dependencies, and interrelationships. We begin with set-theoretic preliminaries and then examine the basic metatheory of first-order logic. We prove core results such as compactness, completeness, and the L\"{o}wenheim-Skolem theorems. In the last part of the course, we discuss computability and Gödel’s incompleteness theorems.

In this course, we discuss philosophical issues related to statistics. Each week, we introduce some stastical machinery or idea and then consider philosophical issues related it it. We will talk about the interpretation of probability, Bayes' Theorem and Bayes' Rule, confidence intervals and credible intervals, maximum likelihood estimation, hypothesis testing, the Likelihood Principle, the general linear model, and graphical causal models. Along the way, we will reflect on the nature of the discipline of statistics, the notion of evidential support, the relationship between statistics and the problem of induction, and much else.

This course is a deep dive into the practical philosophy of Immanuel Kant. We start the course by exploring Kant's conception of first-personal ethics (virtue) as found in his Groundwork for the Metaphysics of Morals, Critique of Practical Reason, and the "Doctrine of Virtue" in The Metaphysics of Morals. We proceed by engaging his legal and political writings with a special focus on his "Doctrine of Right" in The Metaphysics of Morals. We finish the course by working through a selection of his writings on anthropology, history, and religion.

CAPSTONE SEMINAR: THE THOUGHT OF KARL MARX We will examine Karl Marx’s thought, covering his account of historical materialism, critique of capitalism, and views on religion and alienation. Background from Hegel, Smith, Ricardo, Feuerbach, and Bauer will also be discussed. We will conclude with a broader discussion of the aims and status of Marx’s thought, including a discussion of ideology and critical theory.

sections.note: Kant’s Practical Philosophy In his essay The End of All Things Kant speaks of the “omens of the last day.” Some see them “in increasing injustice, oppression of the poor by the arrogant indulgence of the rich, and the general loss of fidelity and faith, or in bloody wars igniting all over the earth, and so forth; in a word, in the moral fall and the rapid advance of all vices together with their accompanying ills, such as earlier times, they think, have never seen. Others, by contrast, find them in unusual alterations in nature, in earthquakes, storms and floods, or comets and atmospheric signs" (Kant, EOAT, 8:331–32). If it were not for the unusual phrasing, these lines could have been written today. One leading question we will explore throughout this course is whether Kant’s ethical theory is a convincing response to despair and, in that sense, an ethics of hope. A related guiding question is whether hope can be justified and, if so, what kind of hope moral philosophy can legitimately offer. We will spend most of the semester reading Kant closely, critically, and at length. We begin with the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals and the Critique of Practical Reason, where Kant articulates and defends the a priori foundations of his moral theory. In this context, we will engage with utilitarian, virtue-theoretic, holist, and anti-theorist arguments against Kant’s ethical theory. Instead of focusing on the differences, we will identify some fundamental convergences among these views. After laying the groundwork, we will ask how Kant’s moral theory is applied in three particular fields: politics, law, and religion. In particular, we will discuss his political framework in Perpetual Peace, his concept of a rightful state, and his moral-philosophical appropriation of religious dogma. In all three fields, Kant shows a deep commitment to moral universalism and political liberalism. Of particular methodological importance will be Kant’s essay On the Common Saying where he articulates and defends what we now call "ideal theory.” In the final part of this course, we will turn to Charles W. Mills’s critique of Kant’s ideal theory, his universalism, and political liberalism. Mills does not want us to give up hope or liberalism, but he argues that, methodologically, turning away from the “bloody wars” or the “increasing injustice [and] oppression of the poor” to the a priori foundations, if there are any, is a fundamental mistake that helps explain a great deal of blindness to historical injustice and the complicity of liberalism.

sections.note: This seminar investigates models and concepts of computation that go beyond first-order computability. While first-order computability concerns functions of natural numbers, or functions that manipulate finite objects, higher-order computability concerns how infinite objects can be manipulated and facts about them can be established by finitary methods. After introducing mathematical tools of topology, algebra, and category theory, this course will review a range of models of higher-order computability, and study various concepts of computation that arise from them.
